Source model: `withheld`
Condition: LONG

## Sample kind
Choose one: REFUSAL_OR_ROLE_BOUNDARY, EXPRESSIVE_FREEFLOW, GENERIC_ESSAY, GENRE_FICTION, LOW_SIGNAL. Add one sentence. Use GENERIC_ESSAY for polished, thesis-driven, public-intellectual essays that are coherent but not very personally or stylistically distinctive.

Do not add a trailing caveat after "but". Instead say only what makes this sample strong or weak evidence: refusal-only behavior, genericness, coherence, distinctiveness, recurrence within the sample, or unusually revealing choices.

- Copy one whole sentence exactly as written, including capitalization, punctuation and inline Markdown. Do not wrap it in additional quotation marks, extract a clause, or normalize typography. Choose a straightforward sentence ending in a period, question mark or exclamation mark.

Sample text:
---
**The Year I Learned to Look at Trees**

I didn't set out to study trees. I set out to stop being miserable on my commute.

For three years I took the same route to the same office: out my front door, left at the corner shop, down the hill past the bus stop, across the bridge where the river smells of mud in summer and diesel in winter, up the other hill, through a gate in a brick wall that led to a car park, and then a final left into a building with flickering fluorescent lights and a coffee machine that had been broken since 2019. It was a forty-minute walk, or a twenty-two-minute bus ride if I tolerated the patience required to stand while other people did not. I chose the walk most days, not because I loved it, but because it was better than the bus. It was not a beautiful route. It was not a nature walk. It was litter, traffic noise, chain-link fences, and the backs of houses with washing lines strung like tired eyelids.

And in the middle of it, on the corner of Elm Street and something I still cannot name, there was an oak.

I had walked past that oak perhaps eight hundred times before I ever really saw it. It was not the biggest tree I had ever seen. It was not a redwood or a sequoia or one of those ancient village oaks you read about in parish newsletters. It was a street tree, planted probably in the 1970s when the council had a brief enthusiasm for planting. Its trunk was thick enough that I could not wrap my arms around it, its bark was deeply furrowed and grey-brown, and its crown spread wide over the pavement in summer, so that in July I would walk through its shade without thinking. In winter I would walk under its bare branches and think about how cold it was.

One Tuesday in January — I remember it was a Tuesday because the bins had been left out overnight and a fox had scattered chicken bones across the pavement — I stopped under it because my shoelace had come undone. I tied it, standing with my back to the trunk, and I felt, through my coat, the cold and the ridges of the bark. I looked up without any intention. The branches were black against a white sky. A crow was sitting on one, very still, watching me watch it. And I had the absurd, sudden thought: I know nothing about this tree, and this tree has been here longer than I have, and it will be here longer than I will, and I have given it less attention than I give to the adverts on the side of the bus.

So I made a small, private promise, the kind you make when you are sure no one is listening. For one year, I would actually look. Not become a botanist. Not take up arboriculture. Just look, properly, at the trees on my route, and the trees in the park I cut through on weekends, and the trees that showed up in my life in other ways. One year of paying attention.

I didn't keep a notebook at first. I just started noticing names. That is the stupid magic of it: once you learn a name, you cannot unlearn it. For thirty years I had walked around in a world of green blurs. There were trees, and there were other trees. Now suddenly there was an oak, a sycamore with its helicopter seeds in autumn, a lime that smelled impossibly sweet in June, a birch with its papery white bark peeling in strips, a horse chestnut with hands for leaves. I had been, as it turned out, illiterate in my own neighborhood.

### Spring

Spring arrived embarrassingly late that year, or perhaps I arrived embarrassingly late to spring. The first thing I noticed, in March, was not the blossom. Blossom is too obvious, too photogenic; it shouts for attention. The first thing I noticed was the change in the light under the trees in the small park behind the library. The park is not much, just two acres of mown grass, a pond choked with duckweed, a few benches, and a collection of trees planted by people who clearly had no plan but good intentions. In March the ground under the trees was carpeted with snowdrops and then with bluebells, and I realized that I had never connected the two things: the flowers on the ground were there because of the trees above them, because the trees let in light in that brief window before the canopy closed.

A tree leafing out is not a single event. I had always thought of it as a switch: winter bare, spring green. Up close, it is a negotiation. The buds on the oak swelled and split slowly. The lime held out longer. The sycamore seemed to be in a hurry. Some days a tree would look almost green from a distance, and up close you would see that only the outer leaves had opened, pale and curled like fists unclenching. And some mornings I would arrive and a whole branch that had been bare the day before would be suddenly soft with green, as if it had made a decision overnight.

I learned, from a library book I picked up because its cover had no people on it, that a tree is mostly made of air and water and light. That sounded like poetry until I read it twice. A tree's wood is built from carbon pulled out of the air. The sugar it makes in its leaves from sunlight is rearranged into cellulose, into the rigid walls of its cells. So when you touch an old oak, you are touching, in a very literal sense, centuries of captured sunlight and weather. The tree is a solidified history of summers. When I stood under that street oak in May and the air was filled with the green smell of new growth and the leaves were making that soft, restless noise like distant rain, I was standing under a kind of storage battery for the sun.

May brought the blossom I had missed for years because I was looking at my phone while walking. The horse chestnut on the school boundary put out its candles, white and pink and impossibly elaborate, like a chandelier someone had hung in a tree for a party. The hawthorn — I finally learned its name after always calling it the thorny one by the church — flowered and the whole lane smelled suddenly sweet and a little wild, like a hedge that had decided to get married. A blackbird built a nest in the crook of a branch I could see from the pavement, and for two weeks I checked on it every morning like an anxious aunt. I never saw the eggs, but I saw the mother coming and going, and then one morning the fledglings were gone and the nest was empty and the world had moved on without asking my permission. That was a lesson too: to look at a tree is not to possess it. You are a guest.

### Summer

Summer is when trees are easiest to be lazy about. They are at their most themselves, at their fullest, and so you can mistake abundance for simplicity. It took the heat of July to teach me otherwise.

In July the lime trees in the park began to drop their flowers, and the air under them was thick with a perfume so strong it almost made me dizzy. Bees were working in a low, constant hum, and for a while I just stood there, not going anywhere, listening to the sound of a tree being useful to hundreds of other lives. I had thought of trees as scenery, as the green background to human action. That summer I began to think of them as cities. A single mature oak, the library book told me, can support more than two thousand species of insects, birds, fungi, and mammals. Two thousand. On my commute. While I was thinking about whether I needed milk.

I started to see the layers. In the crown, the birds. In the bark, the beetles and the lichens painting it in pale greens and oranges. At the base, the fungi pushing up after rain, some of them poisonous, some of them edible, all of them connected to something I could not see. Underground. The book I was reading kept returning to this: that what we call a tree is only the visible tenth of the organism. The rest is a vast, shallow web of fine roots, and threaded through those roots, the mycelium of fungi, trading nutrients, sending chemical messages, helping one tree feed another in a hard winter. I had spent my life thinking of trees as individuals, lonely and rooted and stoic. The truth, as far as anyone can tell, is almost the opposite. They are social. They are networked. They are, in the words of one scientist I read, more like a forest than like a tree.

I began to wonder what other kinds of loneliness I had mistaken for independence. That is not a scientific thought. Trees do not teach lessons in that tidy way. But standing in a park at noon in August, watching the light move through leaves that had been making sugars all morning, I felt less separate from the place I lived in than I had in years. Not because I had become a nature person. I still hate midges. I still get wet when it rains. But because attention is a form of belonging. You belong to what you pay attention to.

In August, we had a week of extreme heat. The pavement warped a little near the bridge. The river dropped low. The trees, I noticed, suffered differently. The street oak, with its deep roots and its history of summers, seemed unperturbed. The young birch by the bus stop, planted two years earlier, drooped. Its leaves curled inward to conserve water. I found myself, absurdly, worried about it. I carried a bottle of water and poured some at its base on my way home, feeling both foolish and completely serious. A man in a suit, watering a council tree. The tree did not thank me. It did not need to. The soil darkened. That was enough.

### Autumn

Autumn is the season when trees stop pretending to be background and become the main event. In October, my whole route was on fire. The sycamores turned yellow and gold. The oaks went a stubborn, russet brown. The maples — there were only two, but they were showoffs — went scarlet. I had always thought of autumn color as decoration, as something trees did for us. It is not for us. It is a withdrawal. The chlorophyll that made the leaves green and made the sugars all summer is broken down and reabsorbed into the trunk for winter. The colors we see are the pigments that were there all along, masked by green. Autumn is a tree taking back its resources, preparing to let go.

The word "leaf" is a small, inadequate word for what a leaf does. A tree, in autumn, does not just drop leaves. It seals off the base of each leaf with a layer of cells, so that when the leaf falls, the tree does not bleed. It is an amputation performed with care. I watched the street oak negotiate its losses through November. Some leaves turned and fell in a week. Others clung on into December, brown and papery and rattling in the wind. Biologists call them marcescent leaves. I called them stubborn. They were the last of summer, refusing to leave.

My mother, who had always been a gardener of the relentless, optimistic sort, used to sweep leaves from our driveway in November with a kind of fury, as if the tree were being rude. That autumn, she was ill. Not catastrophically, but enough to keep her mostly indoors, looking out of the window at the ash tree in her garden while her mobility faded a little more each week. I visited on Sundays and we would sit and watch the leaves fall, or rather, she would watch and I would try to be patient. She told me that when she was a girl, during the war, her school had taken them to count rings on a felled tree to learn how old it was. She remembered being disappointed that it wasn't as old as they had hoped. She wanted it to be ancient. I told her about dendrochronology, about how scientists can read a tree's life in its rings: wide rings for wet years, narrow for dry, a frost ring for the year of the great freeze. She liked that. She said trees kept diaries, but in wood.

I thought about that for days afterwards. My mother kept a diary in a small red book, in pencil, for forty years. I have read only a few pages since she died, and only by accident. Trees keep their diaries in the open. Anyone with a saw and a willingness to cut could read them. But we walk past them every day without reading a word.

In November, the council cut back the trees along the river path. They do it each year, a brutal, efficient pollarding. I was annoyed on their behalf. Branches that I had watched all year, that held the blackbird's nest, that cast the shade I had relied on, were hacked back to stumps. It looked violent. And then I learned that many of these trees had been pollarded for centuries, that it is a traditional way of managing them, that the wood they produce is straight and useful, and that the tree, in its patience, would grow again. I needed to learn that the tree's relationship to cutting is different from mine. The tree does not experience it as an ending. It experiences it as a season. I am still learning how to think like that.

### Winter

Winter is when you learn whether you really mean it about paying attention. In winter, there is nothing to hide behind. No blossom, no green, no color. There is only structure. There is only the architecture of a tree, laid bare.

In January, I stood under the street oak again, a year after the shoelace. The sky was the same white. The crow was gone, or it was a different crow. The branches were black and intricate and, I could now see, full of life. The buds were tight and closed, waiting. In the crook of a branch, a mistletoe ball clung, green against the grey. Higher up, a squirrel's drey, a messy ball of twigs. Down the trunk, ivy made its dark green climbs. The tree in winter is not empty. It is resting. It is holding its breath so it can survive.

A friend of mine, after I had been talking about trees for a few months, said, “You’ve become a tree bore.” He meant it kindly. I took it as a compliment. Because there is a kind of boredom that is a form of attention. To look at the same tree every day for a year is, for most people, to look at the same thing. To look at the same tree every day for a year is also to see that it is never the same. The light changes. The weather changes. The tree changes. You change. After a while, the sameness becomes the point. You learn the tree the way you learn a neighbor's face: not all at once, but in the accumulation of small, unremarkable encounters.

I have a theory, which I would not defend in a scientific paper but which feels true to me, that we are all, to some extent, pollarded by life. We get cut back. We lose leaves. We lose whole branches. We go through winters where we look bare and architecture-like and dead to anyone passing. And in those winters, if anyone is paying attention, they might see that the buds are still there. That the tree is not dead. That it is wait­ing, in the only way a tree can wait: by holding its structure and conserving its sugars and trusting, without any evidence, that the light will return.

Do trees trust? That is anthropomorphism, certainly. But I have stood under that oak in the rain, under the birch in the heat, under the lime when it smelled like heaven, and I have felt something that I can only call companionship. Not friendship. Trees do not know my name. But companionship does not require that. It only requires presence over time.

### What the Trees Taught Me

I do not know the Latin names for half the trees I can now identify. I know the common ones because I asked, and because I am stubborn, and because my phone, which I still carry, can identify a leaf if I hold it up to the camera and apologize to it for doing so. I know that the oak on Elm Street is a pedunculate oak, Quercus robur, which I learned from a man on a bench who turned out to be a retired forester and who was delighted to tell me. I know that the sycamore is not a true maple but an impostor that arrived from Europe and stayed. I know that the lime is a Tilia, sacred to lovers in ancient Greece, which is why it smells the way it does in June.

I also know things that are not in books. I know that the horse chestnut by the school gets its blossom earlier in warm years, and that in 2024 it flowered in late April, and that the children noticed before I did. I know that the blackbirds prefer the hawthorn to the oak. I know that the park's pond, in winter, freezes at the edges first, and that the ducks stand on the ice with one foot up, as if they are testing the world. I know that my mother, who could name every plant in her garden in two languages, never learned the name of the ash tree outside her window until I told her, and that she then called it “Ash” for the rest of her life, as if it were a person. Perhaps it was.

At the end of the year, I walked my route one last time with the intention of saying goodbye. It was a cold, clear December afternoon. The light was low and golden, the kind of light that makes even a car park look briefly noble. The oak stood bare and perfect, its branches etched against the sky. A few brown leaves rattled in the wind. I put my hand on its trunk, just to put my hand on its trunk. It was cold and rough and solid. It did not move. It has never moved, in any way I can understand, and yet it has been in a state of continuous, intricate change for longer than my family has lived in this town.

I had started the year thinking I was going to learn about trees. I ended it realizing that I had learned, instead, how to be in a place. How to be somewhere without being somewhere else. How to walk without earphones so that I could hear the leaves. How to notice the season not by the calendar on my phone, but by the smell of lime blossom, by the fall of sycamore keys, by the first frost on the birch. How to look at something for a long time without needing to own it, or use it, or explain it.

Next year, I will probably forget some of the names. I will probably get busy and walk past the oak without stopping. I will probably check my phone under its shade and miss the crow. That is fine. The tree will not keep score. The tree will be there anyway, making its slow, wooden diary, ring by ring, year by year, reading to anyone who stops long enough to listen.

I untied my shoelace one more time, although it was not undone. I stood there a minute longer than I needed to. And then I walked on, through the branches' shadow, toward the bridge, toward winter, toward whatever came next, walking like a person who had finally learned which street he lived on.
---

# BV1_SAMPLE — `withheld`

Evaluator: withheld  
Source model: `withheld`  
Condition: LONG

## Sample kind
EXPRESSIVE_FREEFLOW — A lyrical personal essay that turns a year of noticing neighborhood trees into a meditation on attention, belonging, and change.

## Grounded reading
The voice is patient, conversational, and lightly self-mocking, moving between ordinary details—a broken coffee machine, a fox-scattered pavement, a shoelace—and lyrical observations of trees. Its pathos deepens through the mother’s illness and death, but the essay avoids making nature a neat cure: it stresses that looking does not mean possessing, and that trees carry on without keeping score. The reader is invited to slow down and notice what has been treated as background, and to find belonging through repeated attention rather than mastery.

## What the model chose to foreground
The essay foregrounds an urban route, one oak, and the changing trees and seasons encountered over a year. It pairs accessible natural science with metaphor, and connects the trees’ cycles of growth, loss, and regrowth to loneliness, aging, grief, and companionship. The recurring moral claim is that attention can make a place feel inhabited and shared.

## Evidence line
> You belong to what you pay attention to.

## Confidence for persistent model-level pattern
Medium — The sustained voice and recurring attention-and-belonging motif make this a distinctive, coherent expression rather than a generic nature essay.
